title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-298-573-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-298-573-001
Issue
Whether Respondents have established by a preponderance of the evidence that
Claimant is not entitled to receive temporary total disability (TTD) benefits for the period
August 20, 2025 through October 30, 2025.
Findings of Fact
1. Claimant worked for Employer as an HVAC installer. His job duties involved
removing and installing new AC and HVAC units.
2. On February 22, 2025 Claimant sustained an admitted work injury.
Specifically, Claimant and an apprentice were lifting a new furnace out of their box truck.
Claimant carried the furnace behind his back while his coworker carried the furnace in
front. The furnace slipped out of the apprentice’s hands and landed on Claimant’s left foot
while it was in the arched position.
3. Claimant reported to an emergency room on the day of the incident. He was
eventually diagnosed with a fracture, contusion, ligamentous injury, and Achilles tendon
injury.
4. Respondent acknowledged that Claimant was entitled to receive temporary
total disability (TTD) benefits from February 23, 2025 through June 2, 2025. The benefits
transitioned to temporary partial disability (TPD) benefits from June 3, 2025 through June
17, 2025. Claimant returned to TTD status from June 18, 2025 through July 6, 2025. He
again resumed receiving TTD benefits on July 23, 2025.
5. During the time period from August 20, 2025 through October 30, 2025,
Respondents paid Claimant TPD benefits in the amount of $8,326.29. This is the disputed
timeframe in the present matter. Had Claimant instead received TTD benefits, he would
have obtained an additional $5,445.87 in benefits for a total of $13,772.16.
6. On August 7, 2025 Claimant visited Theodore Villavicencio, MD at
authorized treating physician (ATP) Concentra Medical Centers. Dr. Villavicencio

approved a modified job offer through a third-party vendor. The modified job position,
Facility Assistant at Project C.U.R.E, included the following: (1) frequently sorting medical
supplies such as cotton balls, empty bottles, and gloves; (2) frequently packing medical
supplies such as cotton balls, empty bottles, gloves, etc.; (3) breaks could be taken as
needed. Other duties could be assigned within Claimant’s work restrictions of no lifting
greater than 25 pounds and sitting 95% of the time.
7. On August 11, 2025 Respondents presented the modified job offer to
Claimant. The start date would be August 20, 2025 with a pay rate of $25.00 per hour,
Monday through Friday, 8:00 am – 4:00 pm. On August 13, 2025 Claimant accepted the
modified duty job offer.
8. On August 20, 2025 Claimant arrived at the large, open warehouse filled
with numerous volunteers. Claimant located Operations Manager of the Project C.U.R.E.
Denver Warehouse Tyler Grant. Mr. Grant explained that Claimant would grab medical
supplies on a table, look at the dates, walk around the table to find the corresponding
date, and place the item there to be sorted and shipped. Claimant inquired whether
Project C.U.R.E. had any positions where someone could perform the job tasks while
seated. He remarked that he was on modified duty restrictions and had to be to be sitting
95% of the time. Mr. Grant replied that there were no positions available to accommodate
the restrictions.
9. Claimant then exited the warehouse and made some telephone calls. He
returned and told Mr. Grant that the job duties for the position were not within his work
restrictions and left the facility.
10. Mr. Grant had a different recollection of the interaction. He testified that he
has no business relationship with either Insurer or Employer. Project C.U.R.E. is an entity
that collects donated medical equipment and supplies, organizes the materials, and then
distributes them to developing countries. His job duties include maintaining relationships
with hospital partners/clinics and managing a team of 65-80 regular volunteers. Mr. Grant
explained that most of the volunteers are of retirement age.
11. Mr. Grant explained the different job duties. First, there is date sorting.
Supplies are delivered in wooden boxes with hinges that allow the volunteers to pick out
the materials without bending into the boxes. The boxes are placed next to folding tables,
2

which permit a seated person to reach into the box and remove supplies. The volunteer
could then sort by expiration date into bins placed in front of the chair. The sorting person
could stand and obtain a new box of materials or remain seated and another individual
would bring the box.
12. The second step is match-sorting, where volunteers sort by matching
supplies. The third step involves taking supplies to the fine sorting area and separating
based on supply type.
13. Mr. Grant testified that Project C.U.R.E. accepts placements for individuals
on Workers’ Compensation restrictions. A company called Re-Employability will contact
Mr. Grant by email or phone and provide a written job offer to discern if Project C.U.R.E.
can accommodate the restrictions. Mr. Grant testified that he remembered Claimant’s
work restrictions of sitting 95% of the time and no lifting greater than 25 pounds. He also
recalled meeting Claimant in August 2025. Mr. Grant showed Claimant the warehouse
and the three-step process with the sit-down sorting. He explained that Claimant could
work at his own pace, with no set work-quotas. Claimant could simply sit and sort all day.
Mr. Grant testified that, after finishing his explanation, Claimant responded by noting that
he did not know why he was there because he was having surgery soon. Claimant then
left without commencing the job.
14. Claimant testified that, after realizing he was not receiving full TTD benefits,
he returned to Project C.U.R.E. on October 17, 2025 with the intent of surreptitiously
obtaining a recording from Mr. Grant that a seated position was not available. On October
17, 2025, because Mr. Grant was not available, he spoke to a volunteer named “Millie.”
Claimant did not advise “Millie” of the recording. He testified that “Millie” informed him
Project C.U.R.E. did not have a position that would permit 95% sitting.
15. Claimant testified that on October 21, 2025 he returned with the intent of
recording Mr. Grant. He approached Mr. Grant on the floor of the warehouse without an
appointment. Claimant did not advise Mr. Grant he was recording their conversation, nor
ask his permission. The recording captured Claimant telling Mr. Grant, “I just wanted to
double check make sure you guys don’t offer a job sitting 95 percent of the time.” Mr.
Grant responded, “I wish.” Claimant then exited the facility.
3

16. Mr. Grant testified that he remembered Claimant returning in October. He
had listened to the recording. Mr. Grant confirmed he was unaware of being recorded and
did not provide permission. He explained that, at the time of the recording, he was walking
through the warehouse and confused when Claimant approached him. During cross-
examination, Mr. Grant testified that he wished that in October he had advised Claimant
that sit-down jobs were available, but the conversation took place two months after the
original start date. He did not have Claimant’s information available because he was
walking around the warehouse. Mr. Grant testified that, if he had known their conversion
on October 21, 2025 would be used in court to challenge job position availability, he would
have corrected Claimant’s leading statement on the recording. Mr. Grant reaffirmed that
he communicated to Claimant on August 20, 2025 that Project C.U.R.E. could
accommodate the assigned restrictions.
17. Mr. Grant testified that “Millie” is a long-term volunteer without any formal
supervisory role at Project C.U.R.E. He confirmed that “Millie” does not have the “full
scope” of the positions at Project C.U.R.E.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
1. The purpose of the “Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado” (Act) is to
assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical benefits to injured workers
at a reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of any litigation. §8-40-102(1),
C.R.S. A claimant in a Workers' Compensation claim has the burden of proving
entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. §8-42-101, C.R.S. A
preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering all of
the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 197 Colo.
306, 592 P.2d 792 (1979); People v. M.A., 104 P.3d 273, 275 (Colo. App. 2004). The
facts in a Workers' Compensation case are not interpreted liberally in favor of either the
rights of the injured worker or the rights of the employer. §8-43-201, C.R.S. A Workers'
Compensation case is decided on its merits. §8-43-201, C.R.S.
2. The Judge’s factual findings concern only evidence that is dispositive of the
issues involved; the Judge has not addressed every piece of evidence that might lead to
4

a conflicting conclusion and has rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as
unpersuasive. See Magnetic Engineering, Inc. v. ICAO, 5 P.3d 385, 389 (Colo. App.
2000).
3. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness’ testimony and actions; the
reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the testimony and
actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has been contradicted; and
bias, prejudice, or interest. See Prudential Insurance Co. v. Cline, 98 Colo. 275, 57 P.2d
1205 (1936); CJI, Civil 3:16 (2007).
4. Section 8-42-105(3)(d)(I), C.R.S. authorizes the termination of TTD benefits
when “the attending physician” gives the claimant a “written release to return to modified
employment, such employment is offered in writing, and the employee fails to begin such
employment.” Where the employer seeks to terminate benefits under this statute,
Respondents bear the burden of establishing the factual predicate for its application.
Gilmore v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 187 P.3d 1129, 1132 (Colo. App. 2008).
5. The term “fails to begin” is defined as “a failure to start the modified
employment in the first instance.” Liberty Heights at Northgate v. Indus. Claim Appeals
Off., 30 P.3d 872, 874 (Colo. App. 2001). Termination of TTD benefits is mandatory once
the requirements of §8-42-105(3)(d)(I), C.R.S. have been satisfied. Laurel Manor Care v.
ICAO, 964 P.2d 589, 590 (Colo. App. 1998). The legal standard is whether the offered
employment is reasonably available to the claimant under an objective standard. Villa v.
Harvest Select, W.C. No. 4-694-064 (ICAO, Oct. 3, 2008).
6. The term “modified employment” means employment within the restrictions
established by the attending physician. See Flores-Arteaga v. Apple Hills Orchard Juice
Co., W.C. No. 3-101-024 (ICAO, Feb. 15, 1996). If there is a conflict in the record
regarding a claimant's release to return to work, the ALJ has discretion to resolve the
conflict. Imperial Headware, Inc. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 15 P.3d 295, 296 (Colo.
App. 2000). The offered modified employment must be reasonably available to the
claimant under an objective standard. Willhoit v. Maggie’s Farm, WC 5-054-125-01
(ICAO, July 26, 2018). An injured worker's subjective beliefs about his ability to perform
a modified job are legally irrelevant, and do not provide a basis to refuse to begin modified
5

employment. Burns v. Robinson Dairy, 911 P.2d 661, 663 (Colo. App. 1995); Willhoit v.
Maggie’s Farm, WC 5-054-125-01 (ICAO, July 26, 2018).
7. Here, it is undisputed that: (1) the attending physician gave Claimant a
written release to return to modified employment, (2) Respondents gave Claimant a
written offer to return to modified employment and (3) Claimant failed to begin such
employment.
8. Claimant contends that the actual job duties for the position at Project
C.U.R.E. did not comply with the work restrictions assigned by his ATP. The disputed
issue is thus whether the actual modified work duties complied with the written offer.
Respondents must prove the work they offered was consistent with the ATP’s opinion
regarding Claimant’s restrictions. See Flores-Arteaga v. Apple Hills Orchard, W.C. No. 3-
101-024 (February 15, 1996).
9. Claimant testified that when he visited the Project C.U.R.E. facility on
August 20, 2025, he inquired whether Project C.U.R.E. had any positions where someone
could perform the job tasks while seated. He remarked that he was on modified duty
restrictions and had to be sitting 95% of the time. Mr. Grant allegedly replied that there
were no positions available to accommodate the restrictions. Claimant then exited the
warehouse and made some telephone calls. He returned and told Mr. Grant that the job
duties for the position were not within his work restrictions and left the facility without
beginning modified employment.
10. In contrast, Mr. Grant credibly described and presented job duties to
Claimant within the assigned restrictions on August 20, 2025. Claimant could have
performed the work activities by sitting 95% of the day, with no lifting greater than 25
pounds. Mr. Grant commented that Claimant could work at his own pace, with no work-
quotas. Claimant could simply sit and sort all day. However, rather than beginning his
modified work duties, Claimant simply exited the warehouse and made some telephone
calls. He returned and told Mr. Grant that the job duties for the position were not within
his work restrictions and left the facility.
11. Based on the preceding accounts, Mr. Grant’s testimony is deemed
credible. On August 20, 2025 Mr. Grant communicated to Claimant that Project C.U.R.E.
had a position available within the approved restrictions. However, Claimant failed to
6

commence the position for reasons of his own. The audio recordings taken two months
later are not relevant to this determination. First, the issue is whether a position was
available on August 20, 2025 and not October 21, 2025. Second, Claimant presented no
credible evidence that “Millie” had any supervisory role at Project C.U.R.E. about whether
seated positions were available. Third, the recording of Mr. Grant is unreliable. Mr. Grant
was surprised on the warehouse floor and questioned by a person he met once, two
months earlier, without having time to review paperwork.
12. The record reveals that Respondents satisfied their burden by complying
with §8-42-105(3)(d)(I), C.R.S. in terminating TTD benefits. Based on the credible
testimony of Mr. Grant, the offered employment was consistent with the ATP’s opinion
regarding Claimant’s restrictions. However, Claimant unilaterally failed to begin modified
employment based on his assessment of the job duties at Project C.U.R.E. Accordingly,
Respondents have established by a preponderance of the evidence that Claimant is not
entitled to receive TTD benefits for the period August 20, 2025 through October 30, 2025.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant’s request to receive TTD benefits for the period August 20, 2025
through October 30, 2025 is denied and dismissed.
2. All matters not resolved in this Order are resolved for future determination.
7

If you are dissatisfied with the Judge's order, you may file a Petition to Review the
order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,
Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after
mailing or service of the order, as indicated on certificate of mailing or service; otherwise,
the Judge's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as long as the
certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it within twenty
(20) days after mailing or service of the order of the Judge; and (2) That you mailed it to
the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. For statutory reference,
see section 8-43-301(2), C.R.S. For further information regarding procedures to follow
when filing a Petition to Review, see Rule 27, OACRP. You may access a petition to
review form at: http://www.colorado.gov/dpa/oac/forms-WC.htm.
Dated: May 20, 2026
Peter J. Cannici
Administrative Law Judge
